---
title: "Setting up a bench"
description: "What a bench needs, and in which order to set it up"
toc: true
---

A bench is one Arduino board running the `UsbIo` firmware, one host computer
that can talk to it, and one language binding for writing analysis scripts
against the recorded data. Nothing about the boards or the host driver is
AMLab-specific — this section is a guided path through
[ArduinoDriver](https://github.com/pbosetti/ArduinoDriver)'s own setup, in the
order that avoids backtracking.

## What a bench needs

- **One supported board** with a USB cable — see the [recommendation
  matrix](#board-recommendation) below and [Supported boards](boards.qmd) for
  the full detail.
- **A host computer.** Linux, macOS and Windows are all supported; the three
  differ in what setup they need and in how good the achieved sampling timing
  is — see [Host operating system](#host-operating-system).
- **The `arduino-io` command line tool and its C++ driver**, built from
  source on the host.
- **A language binding** — [Python](python.qmd), [R](r.qmd), or both — for
  writing the analysis templates the experiments use.
- **For the T\* and M\* experiments**, the conditioning and rig hardware
  described in [Hardware](../hardware/index.qmd).

## Setup order

Each step depends on the one before it, so work through them in order the
first time:

1. **Board and firmware.** Install the Arduino core for your board, upload
   the three-line `UsbIo` sketch, and confirm the board re-enumerates. See
   [Flashing the UsbIo firmware](firmware.qmd).
2. **Host OS preparation.** Linux needs a udev rule installed once; Windows
   needs WinUSB bound to the board's vendor interface with Zadig; macOS needs
   nothing. See [Linux](host-linux.qmd), [macOS](host-macos.qmd) or
   [Windows](host-windows.qmd).
3. **Host driver and CLI.** Build `arduino_driver` and the `arduino-io` CLI
   from the ArduinoDriver repository and put `arduino-io` on `PATH`. The
   per-OS pages above cover this alongside the OS-specific step.
4. **Language binding.** Install the Python or R package that wraps the same
   driver, for writing analysis scripts. See [Python](python.qmd) and
   [R](r.qmd).
5. **Verification.** Confirm the whole chain works end to end: `arduino-io
   info`, a digital write, an analog read, and a short stream test with a
   clean summary line. See [Verifying a bench](verify.qmd).

If something does not work at any step, [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.qmd)
collects the symptoms ArduinoDriver's own documentation names, with causes
and fixes.

## Board recommendation {#board-recommendation}

@tbl-board-matrix lists every board ArduinoDriver documents as compile-verified,
with the properties that matter for choosing one for a bench. "Streaming"
means continuous sampling over a bulk USB endpoint — required by the S1–S3 and
M3 experiments (see [Supported boards](boards.qmd) for the full
per-experiment breakdown). "Windows" means the board's vendor interface can be
bound with WinUSB via Zadig; where it says no, that board cannot be used from
a Windows host at all with `arduino-io`.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why S2 and M3 need more than "streaming: yes"

A board only reports *whether* it can stream, not how fast. The sketch takes
at most one record per `loop()` iteration, so the achieved rate is bounded by
the board's own loop speed — measured so far only on the Portenta H7 (about
32 kHz on one channel, 23.5 kHz on two, with the plain example sketch). S2 and
M3 need a high loop rate as well as streaming support; on any board other than
the Portenta H7, run the [stream verification](verify.qmd) at the rate the
experiment needs before committing a bench to it.
:::

Two further categories exist but are not in the table: boards with a written
transport shim that has not been hardware-verified (RP2040/RP2350 via
`arduino-pico`, ESP32-S2/S3), and boards that cannot run `UsbIo` at all (UNO
R3, Mega, classic Nano, UNO R4 WiFi). See [Supported boards](boards.qmd) for
both, and for the reasons.

## Host operating system {#host-operating-system}

::: {.callout-important}
## Linux is the recommended lab host

Sampling is driven by the sketch's `loop()`, not by a hardware timer, so the
host's own USB scheduling shapes what actually arrives. On Linux the jitter
observed on the reference bench is typically 1–2 µs; on macOS schedule
restarts and device overruns are more common. Windows has not been
characterized the same way for AMLab. One small machine per bench is enough —
a Raspberry Pi running Linux is sufficient; see [Linux
host](host-linux.qmd#raspberry-pi).
:::

All three host operating systems can run `arduino-io` and the language
bindings, and all three are documented — macOS is a fine place to *develop*
analysis code (nothing to install, and the Portenta H7's High-Speed USB
quirk aside, it just works), but for acquisitions where timing matters, set
up the bench on Linux.
